newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Businesses support Bulgaria currency board plan.
newsitem.headline: Businesses support Bulgaria currency board plan.

text.p: Foreign investors and local businesses have welcomed Bulgaria's acceptance of a tough new monetary regime, hoping it will restore much needed stability and confidence in the crumbling economy.

Earlier this week the government said it accepted the currency board plan proposed by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to boost economic recovery by curbing inflation and restoring confidence in the lev currency.
"The Bulgarian economy is in a tailspin dive and what investors need is confidence and stability which a currency board system can guarantee," said Coopers & Lybrand Managing Partner James Kinghorn.
Investors say Bulgaria has the least favourable business climate in the region.

Interest rates are 180 percent, cumulative inflation for the first 10 months of the year reached 195 percent, the domestic debt is an unserviceable 680 billion levs ($1.94 billion), and foreign debt payments of $1.3 billion fall due next year.
Excessive red tape, inconsistent legislation and arbitrarily applied laws also deter foreign investors.
Debt payments and central bank intervention to support the slumping lev have melted foreign exchange reserves to $541 million at the end of October from 1.43 billion a year ago.

"If the currency board is implemented together with a solid reform platform which would speed up privatisation and cut budget spending for lossmaking state enterprises, the chances of recovery will improve," said Kinghorn.

The currency board system is expected to reduce interest rates and curb inflation in the first months of its introduction by matching the amount of national currency in circulation with the central bank's hard currency reserves.
It will also severely curb central bank lending to commercial banks and the government.
Currency boards, pegging the local currency usually to the dollar, have been used by Argentina, Estonia and Lithuania to restore confidence and help defeat hyperinflation.
The system is expected to be implemented early next year after the government and the IMF work out technical details and parliament gives its approval.

Local businessmen, plagued by unpredictability of interest, inflation and exchange rates, which so far have twice overshot budget targets, say the stability provided by a currency board system would encourage their businesses.

"The fact the company owners will not have to revise their business plans every time the lev falls is a sufficient level of stability which would guarantee our operation," Chavdar Selveliev, chairman of Bulgaria's partnership association of small and medium businesses told a news conference on Friday.

Shopkeepers and suppliers went into panic last week after the lev lost 18 percent of its value in one day due to a crisis of confidence which sent Bulgarians rushing to convert their savings to dollars. Many shops closed for the day.
"With a stable exchange rate we will be able to be more responsible to our partners and employees, instead of risking closing the business every time the lev slumps," said Selveliev.
Revenue now eroded by inflation could be invested for upgrading the business, he added.
However, economists have warned that the currency board alone will not resolve the underlying problems of Bulgaria's heavily-indebted economy.

"The monetary measures were in place throughout these years. It is the lagging structural reform and slack bank supervision that brought about this grave crisis," said one resident banker, who declined to be named.
